vision: Gustavo (a working name) is the security view that keeps pace with teams shipping agent-written code: after every release it shows what changed, where the product is exposed and what to fix, without ever blocking the release, and it turns that same evidence into the answers a buyer or regulator asks for.

strategy.direction: Build the release map and sell it on the buyer's question: a non-blocking view of what each release changed and where the product is exposed, whose evidence also drafts the security questionnaire when an enterprise buyer asks. Run it as a done-for-you service for the first teams, and spend the next six weeks mostly on ten conversations outside the studio network, because most of today's evidence comes from two organisations inside it.
why: The most repeated product request is a view: a map of the system's components and exposure, and per release what changed and a few red points to ticket (E3, a studio founder in three calls; echoed by a CTO who found an open endpoint by chance).

Every tool that added review rounds or CI time was removed whatever it found: CodeRabbit and Cubic for latency, Dependabot for living in the release stream, and a 10-minute CI budget was named. Only an off-path product survives.

Money moves when a buyer asks: forms at the compliance desk, 500 questions, contractual pen tests, with an external pen test put at about €5,000. The stated buying test is save money or get compliant faster, which buyer proof passes and a scanner does not.

PR-time security is being given away by the model vendors (Claude Code security review, Claude Code Security) and bundled by a $1B incumbent at $350 a month, so a reviewer or scanner alone is not a business.
Regulation is moving to continuous evidence: CRA reporting within 24 hours from 11 September 2026 presumes knowing what is in each release, which a release map records.
A service first answers the one willingness-to-pay signal on record, a founder who would pay a licence fee to a provider that does the work, and it needs no product to test the price.

sequence.step: Book ten conversations outside the studio network with founders or CTOs of 2 to 20 engineer teams who received a security questionnaire, pen test demand or partner requirement in the last six months. Ask for the last questionnaire, the hours it took and what they paid. Target: ten held, five questionnaires shared.

Concierge release maps for three teams, two in the network and one outside, delivered by hand after each of four releases with an outside-in probe. Target: two of three teams turn at least one red point into a fix.
Draft answers to two real questionnaires from the concierge evidence within 48 hours each, and record time saved and corrections.
Offer a paid first review with release map and questionnaire answers, priced below the €5,000 external pen test anchor, to every team that shared a questionnaire. Target: two paid.
Decision review against the kill criteria: automate the map as a GitHub App that runs after deploy if two teams paid and three kept opening it; otherwise re-plan from the ten conversations.
If continuing, ship the automated release map to the paying teams and the GDPR pack as the first preset.

notNow: Another AI reviewer in the pull request: the teams interviewed removed the ones they tried, and Anthropic gives security review away.
A dependency update bot: contested pain, crowded by Renovate, Dependabot and Aikido autofix.
On-premises or sovereign deployment for regulated vendors: cloud AI is forbidden there and the one buyer sees no ROI.
A full SOC 2 or ISO automation platform against Vanta and Drata; start with answering the buyer, not running the audit.
An autonomous SOC or runtime monitoring: a different buyer, and the founder of the one team interviewed said telemetry is not for him.
Brand, domain launch or public site before a price has been tested; the first ten conversations come from direct outreach and introductions.
killCriteria: Fewer than 4 of the 10 outside teams received a security questionnaire, pen test demand or partner requirement in the last six months: the trigger is too rare at this stage, so move up-market or change the problem.
Concierge maps find nothing a team chooses to fix in 2 of 3 teams: the view has no value beyond reassurance.
Teams stop opening the map after the second release: visibility is wanted in interviews but not used.
By 4 December no team outside the studio network pays for a first review at any price: stop and re-plan.
Teams refuse to connect repositories or infrastructure to a startup: the product needs a code-free entry, or it is not viable.
Aikido or Anthropic ship a release map with buyer answers free before the first paid pilot: narrow to the done-for-you service or stop.
evidenceGaps: How often teams of 2 to 20 engineers actually face a buyer questionnaire or pen test demand: ask all ten conversations, count, by 23 October.
Who pays and from which budget: founder, CTO or sales. Ask about the last security or compliance purchase in every conversation.
Price: nobody has been quoted. Test a single price below the pen test anchor in November.
Whether AI-drafted answers are trusted by buyers: ask the teams who share a questionnaire whether their buyer would accept evidence-backed answers.
Whether the map's findings are repeatable enough to trust, given the non-determinism objection: run the same map twice per release in the concierge phase and compare.
Whether sovereignty changes decisions for small EU teams: one question in every conversation, counted.
Housekeeping: add titles and roles to VSI speakers, fix the misattributed compiled quotes, and record outside calls rather than internal ones.

trends.title: AI writes more code, and its security has not improved
trends.text: Veracode's 2026 tests of over 100 models put the security pass rate of AI-generated code at 56%, barely up from 55%, while AI writes a growing share of committed code. The volume of unreviewed risk grows with adoption.

evidence.text: Average security pass rate 56%, about 44% of tasks introduced a vulnerability.

trends.title: Review, not writing, is now the bottleneck
trends.text: Practitioners describe PR review as the main bottleneck as agents multiply output, and push trivial checks to automation so humans judge intent. A security product that adds to the review queue fights the strongest current in engineering.

trends.title: EU rules move from certificates to continuous evidence
trends.text: Since 11 September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act requires anyone selling software into the EU to report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours, which presumes knowing what is in each release. DORA pulls ICT suppliers of financial firms into threat-led testing. Proof is becoming a running obligation, not a yearly document.

evidence.text: CRA reporting of exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents applies from 11 September 2026, 24 hours for an early warning.

initiatives.summary: After every deploy, a non-blocking map of the system's components and edges, the parts the release changed, and a short list of red points filed as tickets, never a failed build.
initiatives.bet: We believe that small teams shipping with coding agents will keep a security view that costs them nothing in the release path and shows what changed and where they are exposed. Aikido or Anthropic add a release view to tools teams already have.

initiatives.summary: Trace where personal data travels, into logs, observability, third parties and hosting regions, flag leaks on the release map, and produce the evidence a partner asks for under GDPR.
initiatives.bet: We believe that GDPR, the one requirement every partner applies, is a better first pack than SOC 2 for EU teams this early. We will know when 3 teams accept the pack's findings as their record of processing evidence.
initiatives.problem: Logs carry user IDs into self-hosted observability and nobody can tell whether data leaks somewhere non-obvious.
risks: GDPR is mostly legal and process, not code, so the product may cover too little of it.
Privacy tools already map data flows.
The preset-pack request is E2 from one CTO.
initiatives.firstMove: During the concierge reviews, list every personal-data flow found in code and infrastructure and ask each team whether it would hand that list to a partner.

initiatives.title: Security hints inside the coding agent
initiatives.summary: A Claude Code skill or MCP server that knows the system map and tells the agent which security domains a change touches, and which new packages are risky, while it is still writing.
initiatives.bet: We believe that feedback at the moment of change is the only kind agent-first teams keep. We will know when a team keeps the skill installed for a month and its hints change at least one change per week.
initiatives.problem: Findings arrive at PR time or weeks later, when developers are already done; new packages suggested by the agent are adopted unscanned.
risks: OX VibeSec and Anthropic already move into generation time.
Hints add tokens and latency to every session.
Only valuable once the system map exists.
initiatives.firstMove: After the release map works for three teams, expose it as a read-only MCP resource and test it with one team for two weeks.

initiatives.title: One pull request for safe dependency updates, with a verdict
initiatives.summary: Bundle security and minor updates into a single PR, check whether they break the application, and escalate only the risky ones.
initiatives.bet: We believe that teams would drop Renovate's checkbox dashboard for one verdict per week. We will know when a team merges the bundle without opening it for four weeks.
initiatives.problem: Renovate and Dependabot turn updates into box-ticking and PR sprawl.
risks: Parked: the pain is real for one CTO (E4) but the studio founder fixes dependency failures in a minute or two, so it is contested.
Renovate grouping, Dependabot cooldowns and Aikido autofix already chase it.
It would make the venture a dependency tool, far from the release map and buyer proof.
initiatives.firstMove: None now. Revisit if 3 of 10 outside conversations rank dependency updates as a top-three pain.

initiatives.title: Another AI security reviewer in the pull request
initiatives.summary: An AI reviewer that comments on security issues in every pull request, cheaper than CodeRabbit.
initiatives.bet: We believe that a cheaper PR security reviewer wins teams that find CodeRabbit too expensive. We will know when a team replaces its current reviewer with it.
initiatives.problem: CodeRabbit was called very expensive by one team.
risks: Parked: the teams that tried PR reviewers removed them for latency, not price, and one runs a homegrown Claude reviewer that works.
Anthropic ships a security review GitHub Action and Claude Code Security; competing on price with the model vendor is a losing position.
It adds rounds to the loop that is already the bottleneck.
initiatives.firstMove: None. Keep the release map strictly off the PR path.

initiatives.title: On-premises security AI for regulated vendors
initiatives.summary: A self-hosted, small-model version of the product for vendors serving banks and other regulated buyers who cannot use cloud AI.
initiatives.bet: We believe that sovereign buyers will pay for on-premises AI security tooling. We will know when a regulated vendor funds a pilot including its own GPUs.
initiatives.problem: Regulated vendors cannot use cloud AI and doubt generative AI next to deterministic scanners.
risks: Parked: the one regulated buyer sees no ROI, already runs Snyk and SonarQube on premises, and objects to non-deterministic findings.
It needs 8 to 32 billion parameter models on customer GPUs and custom deployments, a different company.
Regulated buyers do not take one-size-fits-all products.
initiatives.firstMove: None now. Keep one question on sovereignty in every conversation and revisit if EU teams make it a buying condition.
